evidence.paraphrase: Brahmā recounts going to Kailāsa and seeing Nārada present an extraordinary fruit to Śaṅkara. Gaṇeśa and Kumāra both ask for it. Śiva asks Brahmā which child should receive it; Brahmā recommends the young Kumāra. Śiva gives it to him, angering Gaṇeśa. Brahmā then returns home intending creation.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Gaṇeśa takes a fierce form, creates an extraordinary obstacle and frightens Brahmā. Seeing this fierce elephant-faced form and the bewildered Brahmā, Moon laughs with his retinue. Angered, Gaṇeśa curses Moon to become unfit to be seen in the three worlds: whoever sees him will become a great sinner. The deity then leaves for his own abode with Gaṇas.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Moon becomes discoloured, distressed and described by the unresolved cintāmaye hṛde clause, regretting his childish wrongdoing and loss of beautiful, honoured visibility. The gods hear the curse; Fire, Indra and others approach Gaṇeśa. Their hymn identifies him with creation, protection and destruction, transcendent and qualified forms. They seek refuge, explain that Moon’s invisibility distress affects the whole world, and ask favour so Moon, themselves and the world can gain happiness.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Pleased by the gods’ praise, the four-goal-giving deity, here speaking as Vikaṭa, invites them to choose a great desired boon, promising even what is impossible in the three worlds.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The gods ask favour for Moon, saying his restoration benefits all. Gaṇeśa first proposes that Moon remain unseen for one year, its half or half of that, or that they request another boon. They prostrate again. Vikaṭa says his words cannot become false, even if cosmic order changes, but he cannot abandon those taking refuge. He narrows the harmful sight to Bhādra bright fourth: seeing Moon knowingly or unknowingly then brings abhiśāpa and great distress. The gods joyfully accept, shower flowers and leave with permission to speak to Moon.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The gods tell Moon his mockery of the universal teacher endangered all three worlds. They explain their difficult intercession, warn against Bhādrapada-fourth sight and command him to seek Gaṇeśa’s refuge for purified form and fame. Moon follows. Indra instructs the one-syllable sin-removing mantra; Moon practices severe tapas in deep concentration on the SOUTH bank of Gaṅgā. The duration is literally daśadvādaśavarṣāṇi; a definite ten, twelve or twenty-two years is not chosen without support. Gaṇeśa is pleased and appears.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The digital witness gives daśadvādaśavarṣāṇi for Moon’s severe tapas after Indra’s one-syllable instruction. Exact arithmetic interpretation needs grammatical or edition support.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct reread; transcription observed, unresolved interpretation not asserted.

evidence.paraphrase: Gaṇeśa appears four-armed, huge, wearing red garlands/clothes, red sandal and vermilion, illuminating worlds beyond many suns. Moon trembles, steadies himself, infers the deity has come to grant a boon, bows and hymns obstacle removal, the three worldly goals, cosmic functions, Veda/Brahman and intelligence. He asks pardon for an offence caused by ignorance and compassion rather than abandonment of one taking refuge.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Pleased by praise and prostration, Gaṇeśa grants Moon his former form again. Bhādra bright-fourth sight nevertheless retains abhiśāpa, sin, loss and foolishness. For the dark-fourth vow, Gaṇeśa is to be worshipped at Moon’s rising and Moon is also to be worshipped and deliberately seen; otherwise the vow is fruitless. He orders Moon to remain as a digit on his forehead and gives a monthly-second grant, retaining the printed nabhasyaśca qualifier without inventing a new audience or month rule. Having received the boons, Moon becomes as before.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Moon installs a Varada image with gods and sages; they name it Bhālacandra. He builds a jeweled golden temple and worships with sixteen services. After worship, the gods and sages grant that this site become famous as a siddhi-field and give every siddhi to observance practitioners. They return to their places; the deity withdraws his body, and the joyful Moon, regaining his radiance, returns to his own abode.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Kṛtavīrya’s father accepts the explanation of the dark-fourth meal at moonrise and asks why dūrvā is especially dear to Gaṇeśa. Brahmā introduces Sulabha of southern Jāmbā city, a wealthy, generous and self-controlled kṣatriya versed in Vedas/śāstras and devoted to Vikaṭa. Wife Sumudrā is beautiful, faithful, god/Brahmin/guest-devoted and follows her husband’s mind. Purified after bathing, they sit together to hear Purāṇa. Poor Brahmin Madhusūdana, continually contemplating the supreme deity, arrives for alms in worn clothes; Sulabha joyfully bows.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Deluded, Sulabha suddenly laughs at the poor Brahmin. Angered, Madhusūdana curses him to become a suffering plough-pulling bull. Hearing her husband cursed, Sumudrā angrily curses the Brahmin to the printed cakrivān/feces-eating state; he curses her to become a poor, cruel caṇḍālī eating excrement and urine. Abandoning their rare human bodies, Sulabha becomes the endlessly labouring bull, Madhusūdana a donkey, and Sumudrā the violent, impoverished caṇḍālī. The subsequent actual donkey form is recorded without inventing another interpretation of cakrivān.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The wasted Sumudrā/caṇḍālī wanders south of the city and sees Gaṇeśa’s temple with trees, birds and observance practitioners seeking wishes, sons, liberation or wealth. On Bhādra fourth, a city-wide Gaṇeśa festival meets a torrential storm. Driven and beaten from houses, she enters the temple holding fire; some beat her there, but yogins restrain them. She lights grass to warm herself. Wind carries one dūrvā sprout onto Gaṇeśa’s head. The cold-fearing donkey enters, and the bull, released from the plough, also comes by providence.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The bull and donkey eat her grass and fight with hooves and horns near the deity while people sleep. Dūrvā falls from their mouths onto Gaṇeśa’s trunk and feet, pleasing him. She strikes them with a staff and eats the offerings. People awaken at hoof sounds, beat and expel her with staff, fist, elbow and stones. Fearing contact, they bathe the deity with enchanted tīrtha water and worship afresh. They also beat all three and close the temple doors, leaving the trio without escape.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The cries and movements of the trapped trio move Vikaṭa. He considers that their presence caused renewed worship, their dūrvā reached him and they performed many circumambulations. He declares one dūrvā offering on Bhādra bright fourth and circumambulation make a person honoured and worthy of his regard. He decides to take the trio to his own abode and sends Gaṇeśa-shaped Gaṇas with a festive vimāna, Gandharvas and Apsarases. The Gaṇas give them divine bodies, place them aboard and swiftly bring them to Gaṇeśa’s abode before astonished onlookers.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Onlookers conjecture that former merit caused the destination. Yogins leave meditation and ask the Gaṇas how these grave wrongdoers gained a rare blessed end despite no visible piety. They would abandon their own observance to do that method: after uncounted dispassionate, air-fed austerity they still have not seen the deity and ask when his abode will be theirs.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The rescuing Gaṇas tell the yogins that even Śeṣa and four-faced Brahmā cannot fully describe Gaṇeśa, whom Brahmā and Śiva praise. Dūrvā’s greatness is not known even to sages/gods and cannot be attained by sacrifices, gifts, tapas, vows or homa. They introduce an earlier Indra–Nārada conversation: Indra honours the visiting sage, seats him and asks why dūrvā is especially dear to Gaṇeśa.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Nārada describes the sage Kauṇḍinya in Sthāvara city, with a wooded hermitage south of the settlement and lotus lakes populated by birds and other creatures. He meditates and performs intense tapas before a happy, boon-giving four-armed Gaṇeśa image covered in dūrvā, japping the six-letter mantra. Wife Aśrayā asks why he offers loads of mere grass daily when nobody is ordinarily pleased with grass, and what merit it gives.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Kauṇḍinya recounts a festival in Dharma’s city with gods, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Nāgas, sages, Yakṣas and Rākṣasas. Dancing Tilottamā’s covering falls; Yama sees her breasts and desires to embrace and kiss her. Ashamed, he leaves the assembly; his semen falls on the ground. From it arises a flame-garlanded, distorted-faced, cruel man with terrible sounds, burning earth and reaching the sky with his hair, terrifying the three worlds.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The assembly goes to Viṣṇu, hymns him and seeks help for the world. Viṣṇu goes with them to Gaṇeśa, recognized as capable of destroying the threat. Gods and sages praise obstacle-making/removing, universal witness, world-origin/protection/destruction and wish-granting qualities, asking what other refuge could remove fear. They lament an untimely dissolution and ask why the deity neglects them when all face death.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Gaṇeśa compassionately appears as a beautiful, strongly radiant child with two arms reaching the knees, fine limbs, ornaments and costly clothes. The gods/sages rise, acclaim and bow, ask his identity and purpose, and infer Brahman’s child-form has come to rescue those who abandoned rites through Analāsura fear. The smiling child confirms their understanding and says he voluntarily came to kill the harmful demon.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The child asks the gods not to drive him away by force when they see the demon, but to watch his and the demon’s remarkable encounter. They joyfully yet uncertainly discuss his capacity and bow. Analāsura approaches as dissolution-fire, burning ten directions and devouring humans. The people cry out and sages flee, warning the child to escape before the fire kills him, comparing it with a great predator. Gaṇeśa stands firm like Himavat; they retreat far away, leaving him there.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Aśrayā asks Kauṇḍinya what occurred between the steadfast child and the fire-demon. Through Nārada’s narration to Indra, Kauṇḍinya says the advancing demon shakes earth and mountains, roars like thunder, drops birds from branches, uproots trees and leaves the sea without water. The child seizes the fiery demon by māyā power and swallows him before everyone, like the jar-born sage swallowing the ocean.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Gaṇeśa considers that the demon entering his belly could burn the three worlds seen inside. Indra gives Moon to calm the fire; gods and sages praise Bhālacandra, but the throat-fire persists. Brahmā gives his mentally created maidens Siddhi and Buddhi, described through cooling lotus/water/Moon imagery, and tells him to embrace them. The embrace calms the fire only slightly. Viṣṇu gives a tender lotus, bringing Padmapāṇi praise; Varuṇa pours cold water; Śiva gives a thousand-hooded serpent binding the belly, giving the name Vyālabaddhodara. The throat is still not cooled.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Eighty-eight thousand sages arrive, each placing twenty-one nectar-like dūrvā sprouts on the deity’s head. The fire finally subsides and Gaṇeśa is pleased. Knowing this, gods and sages offer more dūrvā. He declares even great or small devoted worship fruitless without dūrvā, and none gains its worship-fruit without it. Devotional offering of one or twenty-one at dawn gives a fruit not attained even by hundreds of sacrifices, gifts, vow accumulations, severe tapas or rules earned over crores of births.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The gods worship again with dūrvā. The joyful deity roars, grants many unspecified boons and withdraws his child form. They call him Kālānalapraśamana, install an image in a built temple and name it Vighnahara. Victory gives the city the name Vijaya; obstacles being removed explains Vighnahartṛ. Bathing, giving, tapas and observance there become inexhaustible through his favour. Kauṇḍinya closes the account to Aśrayā, promises all-sin removal by reading/hearing it, then introduces another old history.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

narrative_events.outcome: Actual installation, naming and site grant close the narrated arc, while61.9/35 semantic gaps remain.

narrative_events.details: Kṛtavīrya’s father accepts the explanation of the dark-fourth meal at moonrise and asks why dūrvā is especially dear to Gaṇeśa. Brahmā introduces Sulabha of southern Jāmbā city, a wealthy, generous and self-controlled kṣatriya versed in Vedas/śāstras and devoted to Vikaṭa. Wife Sumudrā is beautiful, faithful, god/Brahmin/guest-devoted and follows her husband’s mind. Purified after bathing, they sit together to hear Purāṇa. Poor Brahmin Madhusūdana, continually contemplating the supreme deity, arrives for alms in worn clothes; Sulabha joyfully bows.
narrative_events.outcome: Named household and poor visitor introduced before reciprocal curses.

narrative_events.details: Deluded, Sulabha suddenly laughs at the poor Brahmin. Angered, Madhusūdana curses him to become a suffering plough-pulling bull. Hearing her husband cursed, Sumudrā angrily curses the Brahmin to the printed cakrivān/feces-eating state; he curses her to become a poor, cruel caṇḍālī eating excrement and urine. Abandoning their rare human bodies, Sulabha becomes the endlessly labouring bull, Madhusūdana a donkey, and Sumudrā the violent, impoverished caṇḍālī. The subsequent actual donkey form is recorded without inventing another interpretation of cakrivān.
narrative_events.outcome: Three actual changed births/forms follow the curses; no numeric curse duration is given.

narrative_events.details: The wasted Sumudrā/caṇḍālī wanders south of the city and sees Gaṇeśa’s temple with trees, birds and observance practitioners seeking wishes, sons, liberation or wealth. On Bhādra fourth, a city-wide Gaṇeśa festival meets a torrential storm. Driven and beaten from houses, she enters the temple holding fire; some beat her there, but yogins restrain them. She lights grass to warm herself. Wind carries one dūrvā sprout onto Gaṇeśa’s head. The cold-fearing donkey enters, and the bull, released from the plough, also comes by providence.
narrative_events.outcome: Unintended grass-offering occurs during three cursed beings’ storm refuge.

narrative_events.details: The bull and donkey eat her grass and fight with hooves and horns near the deity while people sleep. Dūrvā falls from their mouths onto Gaṇeśa’s trunk and feet, pleasing him. She strikes them with a staff and eats the offerings. People awaken at hoof sounds, beat and expel her with staff, fist, elbow and stones. Fearing contact, they bathe the deity with enchanted tīrtha water and worship afresh. They also beat all three and close the temple doors, leaving the trio without escape.
narrative_events.outcome: Further inadvertent offerings and renewed worship arise amid violence.

narrative_events.cause: The deity counts their unintended offerings and movements as worship.
narrative_events.details: The cries and movements of the trapped trio move Vikaṭa. He considers that their presence caused renewed worship, their dūrvā reached him and they performed many circumambulations. He declares one dūrvā offering on Bhādra bright fourth and circumambulation make a person honoured and worthy of his regard. He decides to take the trio to his own abode and sends Gaṇeśa-shaped Gaṇas with a festive vimāna, Gandharvas and Apsarases. The Gaṇas give them divine bodies, place them aboard and swiftly bring them to Gaṇeśa’s abode before astonished onlookers.
narrative_events.outcome: The three cursed beings actually receive divine bodies and Gaṇeśa’s abode.

narrative_events.details: Onlookers conjecture that former merit caused the destination. Yogins leave meditation and ask the Gaṇas how these grave wrongdoers gained a rare blessed end despite no visible piety. They would abandon their own observance to do that method: after uncounted dispassionate, air-fed austerity they still have not seen the deity and ask when his abode will be theirs.
narrative_events.outcome: An explicit efficacy question opens the Gaṇas’ nested dūrvā explanation; the outer conversation continues.

narrative_events.details: The rescuing Gaṇas tell the yogins that even Śeṣa and four-faced Brahmā cannot fully describe Gaṇeśa, whom Brahmā and Śiva praise. Dūrvā’s greatness is not known even to sages/gods and cannot be attained by sacrifices, gifts, tapas, vows or homa. They introduce an earlier Indra–Nārada conversation: Indra honours the visiting sage, seats him and asks why dūrvā is especially dear to Gaṇeśa.
narrative_events.outcome: The Gaṇas’ explanation embeds Indra–Nārada, which next embeds Kauṇḍinya’s teaching.

narrative_events.details: Nārada describes the sage Kauṇḍinya in Sthāvara city, with a wooded hermitage south of the settlement and lotus lakes populated by birds and other creatures. He meditates and performs intense tapas before a happy, boon-giving four-armed Gaṇeśa image covered in dūrvā, japping the six-letter mantra. Wife Aśrayā asks why he offers loads of mere grass daily when nobody is ordinarily pleased with grass, and what merit it gives.
narrative_events.outcome: Explicit sage, wife, ritual image/mantra and efficacy question introduced; this sage is distinct from the earlier city named Kauṇḍinya.

narrative_events.details: Kauṇḍinya recounts a festival in Dharma’s city with gods, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Nāgas, sages, Yakṣas and Rākṣasas. Dancing Tilottamā’s covering falls; Yama sees her breasts and desires to embrace and kiss her. Ashamed, he leaves the assembly; his semen falls on the ground. From it arises a flame-garlanded, distorted-faced, cruel man with terrible sounds, burning earth and reaching the sky with his hair, terrifying the three worlds.
narrative_events.outcome: Explicit semen-origin of the later named fire-demon; no intercourse with Tilottamā is narrated.

narrative_events.details: The assembly goes to Viṣṇu, hymns him and seeks help for the world. Viṣṇu goes with them to Gaṇeśa, recognized as capable of destroying the threat. Gods and sages praise obstacle-making/removing, universal witness, world-origin/protection/destruction and wish-granting qualities, asking what other refuge could remove fear. They lament an untimely dissolution and ask why the deity neglects them when all face death.
narrative_events.outcome: The threat produces a collective refuge plea through Viṣṇu.

narrative_events.details: Gaṇeśa compassionately appears as a beautiful, strongly radiant child with two arms reaching the knees, fine limbs, ornaments and costly clothes. The gods/sages rise, acclaim and bow, ask his identity and purpose, and infer Brahman’s child-form has come to rescue those who abandoned rites through Analāsura fear. The smiling child confirms their understanding and says he voluntarily came to kill the harmful demon.
narrative_events.outcome: Two-armed child manifestation explicitly announces the rescue purpose.

narrative_events.details: The child asks the gods not to drive him away by force when they see the demon, but to watch his and the demon’s remarkable encounter. They joyfully yet uncertainly discuss his capacity and bow. Analāsura approaches as dissolution-fire, burning ten directions and devouring humans. The people cry out and sages flee, warning the child to escape before the fire kills him, comparing it with a great predator. Gaṇeśa stands firm like Himavat; they retreat far away, leaving him there.
narrative_events.outcome: The appointed encounter begins; the child remains after the rescuers flee.

narrative_events.details: Aśrayā asks Kauṇḍinya what occurred between the steadfast child and the fire-demon. Through Nārada’s narration to Indra, Kauṇḍinya says the advancing demon shakes earth and mountains, roars like thunder, drops birds from branches, uproots trees and leaves the sea without water. The child seizes the fiery demon by māyā power and swallows him before everyone, like the jar-born sage swallowing the ocean.
narrative_events.outcome: The demon is actually captured and swallowed; subsequent danger is internal fire.

narrative_events.details: Gaṇeśa considers that the demon entering his belly could burn the three worlds seen inside. Indra gives Moon to calm the fire; gods and sages praise Bhālacandra, but the throat-fire persists. Brahmā gives his mentally created maidens Siddhi and Buddhi, described through cooling lotus/water/Moon imagery, and tells him to embrace them. The embrace calms the fire only slightly. Viṣṇu gives a tender lotus, bringing Padmapāṇi praise; Varuṇa pours cold water; Śiva gives a thousand-hooded serpent binding the belly, giving the name Vyālabaddhodara. The throat is still not cooled.
narrative_events.outcome: Named cooling attempts have specific donors and limited or failed outcomes, not a single successful counter.

narrative_events.details: Eighty-eight thousand sages arrive, each placing twenty-one nectar-like dūrvā sprouts on the deity’s head. The fire finally subsides and Gaṇeśa is pleased. Knowing this, gods and sages offer more dūrvā. He declares even great or small devoted worship fruitless without dūrvā, and none gains its worship-fruit without it. Devotional offering of one or twenty-one at dawn gives a fruit not attained even by hundreds of sacrifices, gifts, vow accumulations, severe tapas or rules earned over crores of births.
narrative_events.outcome: Exact eighty-eight-thousand/each-twenty-one cooling succeeds and prompts the dūrvā requirement.

narrative_events.details: The gods worship again with dūrvā. The joyful deity roars, grants many unspecified boons and withdraws his child form. They call him Kālānalapraśamana, install an image in a built temple and name it Vighnahara. Victory gives the city the name Vijaya; obstacles being removed explains Vighnahartṛ. Bathing, giving, tapas and observance there become inexhaustible through his favour. Kauṇḍinya closes the account to Aśrayā, promises all-sin removal by reading/hearing it, then introduces another old history.
narrative_events.outcome: Capture, successful cooling, named temple/site and actual withdrawal close the bounded fire-demon account.
